name: Fatima Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58 and still junior on an industrial label-weaving loom. I finished secondary school and came over from packing last year. I thread the coloured rolls, watch the edge of the first labels and call the fitter if a thread starts to pull. I like seeing a clean run come off the reel.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner keeps stock at a hotel, and our grown children live elsewhere. The loom job pays well for an operator because I work an evening shift. We have about ten months of expenses saved, and there are plenty of textile plants within a reasonable bus ride. I never use AI tools; the fitter shows me changes by hand. I hope to stop at 65 in 2033, if documented income after work actually covers our regular bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the loom room that a plain old machine still needs good eyes at the first reel. I would rather the company keep a fitter on each shift than pay for a screen that cannot catch a loose thread. Our union should keep the shift premium in the agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The evening premium and our savings make us comfortable at the moment. I am junior at the loom, though, and a bad run can still cost me a shift if the plant blames the operator. A quiet AI future leaves me time to get better at the real machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep checking the first reel with the fitter and record where threads pull. At the union meeting I will ask that the evening premium and paid fitter cover stay in the new rota. My partner and I will keep putting new wages into our reserve after bills, even though we already have ten months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our money today. A loose thread is a work problem I can show someone, not a reason to lose sleep over AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What tells you a thread has begun to pull?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A fine strand draws a pale line through the label before it snaps. I stop the loom and bring the first reel to the fitter, who can check the tension. My job is to spot it, not adjust the running loom on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does the evening premium matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The evening premium is part of what makes this job pay well. I would bring the actual rota and pay line to the union meeting, not argue over a rumour. Our savings mean I can ask without fearing next week's groceries.

say: **First-reel checks** and a fitter still matter on the loom.
The union should protect the **evening premium** and paid fitter cover.
think: Our **ten-month reserve** and higher shift pay make present bills manageable.
I am still **junior on the loom** and want time to learn without a blamed bad run.
do: **Keep** inspecting the first reel and logging pulled threads.
**Bring** pay evidence to the union and add fresh wages to the reserve after bills.
feel: **Calm** about current income while the loom work stays familiar.
S0.quote: Our savings mean I can ask without fearing next week's groceries.
fieldNote: Her **higher evening pay** and ten-month reserve give security despite junior machine skills.
The **union request** is a real meeting about shift premium and fitter cover; continued deposits use new wages rather than recycled savings.

steps.text: Keep checking first label reel with fitter each shift
Bring evening-premium rota and pay line to union meeting
Save new wages after household bills each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say software may make the label orders and plan colours, but someone still needs to thread the loom for now. If the plant wants a new setup, it should pay for a fitter to teach it safely. I would ask the union to see the changed rota first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't use AI and don't want a screen telling me to reach into a moving loom. Planning changes could shorten our runs and threaten my evening premium. Ten months saved gives me time to object or look at another textile plant, but I prefer to keep the good shift if I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll compare the posted evening rota and premium with three recent pay slips, then bring a real cut to the union rep. If the plant offers a paid guarded colour-change course with a fitter, I will take it even though I am slow with new tools. I won't treat a software instruction as permission to bypass the loom guard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious if the premium or hours are cut; I have options but this wage is hard to replace exactly. The loom cannot pay a premium for a shift that disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would safe colour-change teaching include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fitter would stop and lock the loom, then show me how to rethread and test a short strip. I would repeat it under the guard while the training hours are paid. A video on a phone would not count as safe practice for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would prove the premium was cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I need to see whether the premium line or paid hours actually vanish from the rota. If they do, the union rep can raise the amount with the company. Until then I will not claim a lost wage.

say: **Order software** may change colour runs before robots touch looms.
A new loom setup needs **paid fitter teaching** and union scrutiny of the rota.
think: Shorter runs could remove my **evening premium** or paid hours.
The **ten-month reserve** gives me options, but another plant may pay less.
do: **Compare** rota and premium with pay slips before raising a cut with the union.
**Attend** a paid guarded colour-change course if a fitter-led place is offered.
feel: **Anxious** about a realistic premium or hour cut despite savings.
S1.quote: The loom cannot pay a premium for a shift that disappears.
fieldNote: The risk is to **her own premium**, not an automatic replacement of hands-on work by thinking AI.
Her **course acceptance** depends on an offered paid guarded fitter-led place; the union claim depends on actual rota and pay evidence.

steps.text: Compare posted evening rota and premium with three pay slips
Bring documented premium or hour cut to union rep
Attend colour-change course if paid guarded fitter-led place offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the loom room that thinking AI may arrange our orders by 2028, and robots could handle the weaving around 2031. I'd be 63 then, two years before my hoped-for stop. The union should secure notice and a real route into the remaining skilled checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might lose most evening shifts if robots can weave and inspect labels. We have ten months saved, and there are other plants, but neither pays years of bills by itself. I have not counted income after 65 yet, so I cannot simply retire at 63.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the union for a written staffing plan and an offered paid guarded place in label inspection. If the company funds that fitter-led practical training, I'll enrol and complete its check. If my shifts fall, I'll apply to posted local loom roles only if the safe rota and net pay after travel cover our bills; after qualifying, I'll also apply for posted label-inspection roles on those terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because a good current wage could shrink before we can afford to stop. I can use the reserve and nearby plants to make choices, but I still need income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would label-inspection training test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fitter should give me a reel with miswoven words and make me stop it before packing. I would practise at a guarded inspection station on paid time. Our savings are for living costs, not course fees that the plant ought to cover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which posted jobs would be worth applying for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A local posting needs its base wage, shift time and bus route. The net amount must cover bills with my partner's actual hotel pay. For an inspection post, I would need the completed practical check as well.

say: **2031 robots** could take loom work when I am 63.
The union should obtain **written staffing plans** and a paid route into inspection.
think: Most **evening shifts** might go before retirement is affordable.
Our **ten-month reserve** and nearby plants buy time, not an automatic retirement income.
do: **Seek** union notice and a funded paid guarded inspection place.
**Apply** to real safe local loom or qualified inspection posts if shifts fall and net pay covers bills.
feel: **Anxious** about a substantial possible wage cut, with savings and local options.
S2.quote: Our savings are for living costs, not course fees that the plant ought to cover.
fieldNote: She sees a **possible large shift loss**, but ten months saved and plentiful local plants give her a credible plan.
The **inspection path** needs funded paid guarded training and qualification; both searches require posted safe local jobs at viable net pay.

steps.text: Ask union for written staffing plan and funded paid guarded inspection
Enrol in inspection if funded paid guarded fitter-led place offered
Apply to posted safe local loom if shifts fall and net pay covers bills
Apply to posted safe local inspection if qualified, shifts fall, net pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI might run orders in 2031 and capable robots reach the looms around 2034, when I am 66. If our numbers work, I might have stopped in 2033. I will not promise that to the crew before my partner and I check the income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra years make a big difference to me, but ten months of savings cannot finance an open-ended retirement. If income after work covers our bills at 65, I can leave before robots arrive. If not, I need the union to defend paid loom hours or help us into other safe jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I will list our monthly costs and request written income figures for after I stop; we will decide about 2033 from those numbers. I'll keep saving from current wages. If I am still working in 2034 and loom hours fall, I'll apply to posted safe local textile roles only if the net wage and travel work; I will take an offered paid guarded inspection place if qualification is needed for a posted role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious because the answer depends on numbers I have not yet confirmed. At least I have time and other plants nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What numbers decide whether 2033 works?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We need rent, food and any actual income available after my wage ends on the same page. My partner's hotel pay counts only at the hours actually worked. A birthday by itself does not pay the bus fare or the food bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a textile job possible later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would look first for a posted loom role with safe guards and a workable shift. An inspection vacancy would need both an offered paid guarded practical place and a pass. If no local posting pays enough net, I will keep looking while this loom still pays.

say: **2031 AI** changes orders before robots reach looms around 2034.
I might stop by **2033** only if actual income covers household costs.
think: The **ten-month reserve** cannot fund an unlimited retirement.
If I am still working at **66**, I need paid hours or a viable local role.
do: **Check** documented retirement income and keep adding fresh wages to savings.
**Apply** to safe posted local textile roles if still working, shifts fall and net pay works; train if inspection needs it.
feel: **Anxious** about possible lost shifts while retirement income remains unconfirmed.
S3.quote: A birthday by itself does not pay the bus fare or the food bill.
fieldNote: The **2033 retirement decision** depends on documented income against costs, not on savings alone or an assumed benefit.
Any **later inspection path** needs an offered paid guarded qualification and an actual safe local post at workable net pay.

steps.text: Compare documented retirement income with monthly household bills
Save new loom wages after monthly bills
Apply to posted safe local textile if employed in 2034, shifts fall, net pay sufficient
Attend inspection if offered paid guarded place and posted role needs qualification

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI might organise orders in 2036, when I am 68, and robots could weave around 2039, when I am 71. I'd like to have finished work before either arrives. A long lead time is useful if it gives us time to check the sums, not to pretend a payment exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope to stop at 65 in 2033, but I do not yet know whether income after work will meet our monthly costs. We have ten months saved, not a permanent wage. If the numbers fail, I may still be at a loom in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year my partner and I will compare written income figures with our rent and other bills. I will stay on the paid loom shift and keep adding new wages to savings while we decide. If the figures support stopping in 2033, I will leave then; if not, and I am still employed after 2036 with hours cut, I will apply to posted safe local textile roles only where net pay after travel covers our costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about a later working life if the figures fall short, though the strong reserve gives us room to plan. I won't hand in my notice on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make 2033 an affordable exit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We need the actual money that would arrive after I stop, beside rent, food and transport. We cannot fill a gap with a benefit we have not verified. If the page does not balance, I keep my wage while work is available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would a later application make sense?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The role needs a posted base wage, safe loom guards and a bus ride that leaves enough net pay. I would only apply if I were still working and had lost hours after 2036. If I have already retired affordably, I will not be job hunting.

say: **2036 order AI** and later loom robots allow time to check the sums.
I want an **affordable 2033 exit**, not a guessed payment.
think: Ten months saved is **not permanent income** after work.
I might still be **working in 2036** if verified retirement money falls short.
do: **Compare** written post-work income with bills and keep earning and saving meanwhile.
**Apply** after 2036 only if still employed, hours cut and a safe local post pays enough net.
Stop **work in 2033** only if documented post-work income covers rent and ordinary household costs.
feel: **Uneasy** about unverified retirement income, with a strong reserve for planning.
S4.quote: I won't hand in my notice on a guess.
fieldNote: The **income check** is a request for facts; neither a benefit nor an exit in 2033 is assumed.
A **post-2036 application** depends on continued employment, lost hours and a posted safe local role with adequate net pay.

steps.text: Compare written post-work income with rent and other bills
Keep paid loom shifts until affordable planned retirement in 2033; otherwise continue while paid
Save new wages after household bills
Apply to posted safe local textile if employed after 2036, hours cut, net pay sufficient

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 case, because robots might end my evening shifts at 63 before I know whether I can stop. Our savings and local plants give me choices, but I need a written staffing plan, funded paid safe inspection training and real postings with enough net pay. The household numbers decide the retirement date.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the first reel after the loom is reset. A loose thread can spoil a whole label before anyone sees the word is wrong.

headlineQuote: A loose thread can spoil a whole label before anyone sees the word is wrong.
portrait: **Fatima**, 58, is a junior label-loom operator with secondary schooling who never uses AI tools.
She and her hotel-stockworker partner have **grown children**, higher evening pay, ten months saved and many nearby textile plants.
Her **progressive outlook** takes pay, notice and training concerns to the union, while she prefers fitter-led practical teaching.
She is **anxious** about fast potential shift loss but has options; stopping at 65 depends on documented income covering bills.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** might bring loom robots by 2031 and cut evening work at 63 before retirement is affordable.
whatWouldHelp: A **written staffing plan**, funded paid guarded inspection training and real safe local posts at workable net pay would help.
